source.title: A modern look at the relationship between sharpness and generalization
source.authors: Maksym Andriushchenko; Francesco Croce; Maximilian Mueller; Matthias Hein; Nicolas Flammarion

record.tranche_reason: The study directly evaluates whether adaptive sharpness tracks generalization and reports that the relationship depends on model family and training subgroup; its CIFAR-10 results qualify the claim.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the CIFAR-10 comparison relevant to V7. The paper also reports many other sharpness definitions, radii, datasets, and model settings; those are outside V7’s specific convolutional-family comparison. Its ImageNet, CLIP, and BERT results are not rows for V7.
record.test_reason: The study directly evaluates magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation sharpness against generalization in low-training-error ResNet-18 models on CIFAR-10. It finds strong correlations within training subgroups but weak or reversed correlations when subgroups are pooled. This qualifies V7 using related sharpness measures and an expanded training recipe, rather than reproducing its exact comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that reparametrization-invariant sharpness is not a reliable generalization indicator across their modern settings. Positive correlations occur in restricted ResNet training subgroups, but do not reliably extend to pooled models; the relationship depends on data, architecture, initialization, and sharpness definition.
record.recipe_differences: Measures adaptive sharpness, with and without logit normalization, and correlates it with test error across model pools; the claim’s magnitude-aware sharpness comparison is not reproduced exactly.
record.method_sensitivity: Correlation varies with architecture, augmentation × mixup subgroup, sharpness definition, perturbation radius, and logit normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Adaptive sharpness often has weak or negative associations with generalization for ViTs, fine-tuned CLIP, and BERT, including sharper models performing better under distribution shifts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive sharpness does not consistently predict held-out or out-of-distribution performance across transformer training and fine-tuning settings.

fits_no_version.finding: In sparse regression with diagonal linear networks, adaptive average-case sharpness correlates positively with test loss, while adaptive worst-case sharpness correlates negatively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which sharpness definition predicts generalization depends on the data distribution and predictor parameterization.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 202, 2023
record.problems: The reported CIFAR-10 evidence is correlational. Models are selected for ≤ 1% training error, and the claim’s exact magnitude-aware measure is not tested. The text gives qualitative within-subgroup strength but no exact coefficient for that result.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained: the text’s other CIFAR-10 sharpness definitions, radii, and architectures do not add a separate result for V7’s stated convolutional-family measure. Results for other datasets and model families are outside this version.

untested.parts: Width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Controlled held-out comparisons of adaptive optimizers with SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Training batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets. The m-sharpness ablation changes the sharpness evaluation batch size.
Dropout's effect on held-out error in fully connected or convolutional classifiers.

The exact original perturbation-tolerance measure; superiority over norm- and margin-based measures; SVHN; and an exact replication restricted to training without augmentation. Generalization gaps are inferred from low training error for CIFAR-10 rather than numerically reported for these rows.
Removing highly memorized training examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V7. Adaptive sharpness scales perturbations by weight magnitudes, so it bears on V7 despite differing from the original measure. Other definitions, radii, architectures, and datasets were explicitly declared in rows_left_out and therefore are not listed as undeclared missing results. Their exclusion should not imply agreement across measures: Table 3 reports unnormalized adaptive worst-case ℓ∞ correlation τ = −0.36 at ρ = 0.001. The two retained rows alone do not summarize that measure sensitivity.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and optimizer tuning.
Batch-size effects on the generalization gap.

The study evaluates adaptive sharpness, not the exact magnitude-aware perturbation measure in the version; it reports test-error correlations, with the appendix stating that CIFAR-10 generalization-gap trends are almost identical because included models have ≤ 1% training error. It does not establish causation.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNets-18
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch on CIFAR-10; models shown have ≤ 1% training error
rows.operation_detail: Compared normalized ℓ∞ adaptive worst-case sharpness with test error across models, including models with different augmentation and mixup settings.
rows.measure: Kendall rank correlation between sharpness and test error; authors say cross-subgroup sharpness does not correctly capture generalization.
rows.note: The paper says the generalization-gap trend on CIFAR-10 is almost identical to test error because training error is ≤ 1%. The specific τ is reported for test error.
rows.check: The radius is wrong: normalized adaptive worst-case ℓ∞ sharpness has τ = 0.30 at ρ = 0.001, not 0.0005 (Figure 5; Table 3). This coefficient pools all retained ResNet models; it is not computed exclusively from between-subgroup comparisons. Training also varies learning rate and SAM radius. The pool includes augmentation and mixup, extending V7's stated setting without augmentation.

source_check.correct: Logit-normalized adaptive worst-case ℓ∞ sharpness: pooled CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 Kendall τ = 0.30 at ρ = 0.001; τ = 0.29 at the stated ρ = 0.0005. The coefficient pools retained models rather than measuring exclusively between-subgroup comparisons.
source_check.problem: The reported coefficient belongs to a different perturbation radius.

rows.subject: ResNets-18
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch on CIFAR-10; models shown have ≤ 1% training error
rows.operation_detail: Compared normalized ℓ∞ adaptive worst-case sharpness with test error within subgroups defined by augmentation and mixup settings.
rows.measure: Correlation between sharpness and test error within subgroups; authors describe it as strong.
rows.value: strong correlation; exact value not stated in the text
rows.note: The authors report that ResNets show strong correlation within each training-parameter subgroup, but that this does not carry over across subgroups. Appendix B says CIFAR-10 gap trends are almost identical to test-error trends.
rows.check: The qualitative within-subgroup result is supported. Specify fixed augmentation × mixup settings, with learning rate and SAM radius varying within groups. For the normalized ℓ∞ result highlighted in Figure 5, ρ = 0.001. No numerical within-subgroup coefficient is supplied. Test-error correlation approximates gap correlation according to Appendix B; training error ≤ 1% does not itself establish similarly low training loss.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1, Observations; Figure 5; Appendix H.4; Appendix B.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 models within fixed augmentation × mixup subgroups
relationships.reason: R2 reports strong positive sharpness–test-error correlation within subgroups, including the subgroup without augmentation or mixup; Appendix B says gap trends are nearly identical. This supports the correlational component using a related measure.
relationships.display_finding: Sharpness strongly tracked test error within subgroups, including models without augmentation or mixup, and gap trends were nearly identical.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 models pooled across augmentation × mixup settings, using logit-normalized adaptive worst-case ℓ∞ sharpness at ρ = 0.001
relationships.reason: R1 gives only τ = 0.30, and the authors explicitly report failed ranking between subgroups. Extending the relationship across these training recipes therefore requires qualification; this does not refute V7's narrower setting without augmentation.
relationships.display_finding: Across the pooled models, sharpness had a correlation of τ = 0.30 with the generalization gap at ρ = 0.001. Sharpness did not consistently rank the augmentation and mixup subgroups.

tranche.reason: The study directly investigates sharpness versus generalization and finds that positive within-recipe associations fail to extend reliably across pooled training recipes, qualifying broader applications of V7.
